_about: Per-phase cheat sheet. Each entry's id is also its skill id in the skills table, so never change or reuse an id. what = one-line summary; def / model / game (+gameCode) = the three explainer tabs; aliases = exact inline-code texts that link to this entry; match = regex tested against inline code.

phase1.what: The MSVC compiler. Turns a .c file into an .exe, or stops and prints errors.
phase1.def: cl.exe is Microsoft's C/C++ compiler driver. It preprocesses, compiles each source file to an object file (.obj), then invokes the linker to produce an executable.
phase1.model: A strict translator at a passport desk: hand it your text, and it either stamps out a working program or hands it back with a list of everything wrong.
phase1.game: Every version of the ASCII Runner goes through cl. When you add runner.c in Phase 4.5, cl compiles both files and links them into one runner.exe.

phase1.what: cd moves the terminal into a folder; dir lists what's in it. Be in your repo folder before compiling.
phase1.def: cd (change directory) sets the shell's current working directory; dir lists the files and folders in it. Commands like cl look for files relative to that directory.
phase1.model: You're standing in one room of a house. cd walks you to another room; dir looks around the room you're in.
phase1.game: If cl says it can't find guess.c, you're in the wrong room. dir shows what's here; cd into your game-dev-exercises folder first.

phase1.what: Pastes a header in before compiling, so you can use what it declares.
phase1.def: #include is a preprocessor directive that inserts the contents of another file — usually a header of declarations — at that point before compilation.
phase1.model: Borrowing a toolbox. The toolbox (stdio.h) doesn't do any work itself; it tells the compiler which tools exist and how to hold them.
phase1.game: The runner needs three toolboxes: stdio.h for printf, conio.h for keys and windows.h for Sleep. Leave one out and those names don't exist.

phase1.what: Where every C program starts. Its return value goes back to whatever ran it.
phase1.def: main is the function where a hosted C program starts executing. It returns an int exit status to the environment that ran it.
phase1.model: The front door. However big the program gets, every run walks in through main and leaves through its return.
phase1.game: In the runner, main is just the frame loop. Everything else (reset, update, render) is a function main calls.

phase1.what: Prints text. % slots are filled, in order, by the values after the comma.
phase1.gotcha: Never adds a newline for you.
phase1.def: printf writes formatted output to standard output. Its first argument is a format string; each conversion specification (%d, %s…) consumes the next argument.
phase1.model: A fill-in-the-blanks form. The quotes are the form, the % signs are the blanks, and the values after the comma fill them in order.
phase1.game: The runner's whole renderer is one printf: the lane and the score, drawn over the previous frame.

phase1.what: Escape sequences inside strings: newline, back to start of line, tab, one backslash.
phase1.def: Escape sequences are backslash-prefixed character codes inside string and character literals that represent characters you can't type directly, like newline (\n) or carriage return (\r).
phase1.model: A backslash means "the next character is a control, not a letter" — like a shift key for meanings.
phase1.game: \n moves down a line, which would make the runner scroll. \r jumps back to the start of the same line so the next frame paints over the last one.
phase1.gameCode: printf("\r%s", lane);   // redraw in place, no \n

phase1.what: %d is a whole-number slot in printf. %% prints one percent sign.
phase1.def: %d is the printf conversion for a signed int in decimal. %% is the conversion that outputs a literal percent sign.
phase1.model: %d is a slot shaped for whole numbers. %% is how you write a percent sign on a form where % already means "blank goes here".
phase1.game: Score and frame count are ints, so they print with %d. A progress readout like 75% needs %d%%.
phase1.gameCode: printf("Score: %d  (%d%% of best)\n", score, score * 100 / best);

phase1.what: Ends main and tells the OS the program succeeded. Anything else means failure.
phase1.def: return ends the current function and hands a value back to its caller. Returning 0 from main reports successful termination to the host environment.
phase1.model: Handing in your answer and leaving the room. From main, 0 means "all good", anything else means "something went wrong".
phase1.game: When the player presses Q the runner leaves the loop, prints the final score, and returns 0 — and build.bat-style scripts can check that.

phase1.what: Ends every statement. A missing one is the most common first error.
phase1.def: In C a semicolon terminates an expression statement or declaration. Control structures like if and while are not followed by one unless you mean an empty statement.
phase1.model: The full stop at the end of a sentence. The compiler reads until it finds one.
phase1.game: while (_kbhit()); with a stray semicolon would loop on nothing forever, draining no keys. One character, frozen game.

phase1.what: An error stops the build. A warning (like C4244) builds anyway unless /WX turns it into an error.
phase1.def: A compiler error is a diagnostic that prevents an object file from being produced. A warning is a diagnostic that still allows compilation, unless /WX treats warnings as errors.
phase1.model: An error is a locked door. A warning is a sign on an open door saying "are you sure?" — /WX locks that door too.
phase1.game: Storing a float position into an int lane column raises C4244. Under /WX the runner won't build until you cast on purpose.
phase1.gameCode: int col = (int)x;   // the cast clears C4244

phase1.what: A batch file holding your compile command, flags and files. Type build to run it.
phase1.def: A batch file (.bat) is a Windows script: a text file of shell commands run in order. build.bat holds the project's compiler flags and source list so one command builds everything.
phase1.model: A recipe card for your game: ingredients (the .c files), oven settings (the flags), and one instruction — bake.
phase1.game: Phase 4.5 adds runner.c to the SOURCES line. Nothing else changes; you still type build.

phase1.what: Most warnings · warnings are errors · debug info (PDB) · no optimisation while developing.
phase1.def: /W4 sets the warning level to 4, /WX treats warnings as errors, /Zi emits debug information to a PDB, and /Od disables optimisation.
phase1.model: Turning the smoke detectors to maximum sensitivity, making every alarm stop the build, and leaving a map for the debugger.
phase1.game: /Zi is what lets you set a breakpoint in runner_update and watch r->score change. /Od keeps the code matching your lines.

phase1.what: The exit code of the last command. 0 means it worked; build.bat checks it.
phase1.def: %ERRORLEVEL% is a cmd.exe variable holding the exit code of the most recently run program. By convention, 0 means success.
phase1.model: The thumbs up or thumbs down the last program gave as it left.
phase1.game: build.bat checks it right after cl, so a failed build stops before you accidentally run last week's runner.exe.

phase1.what: Stage changes, save a labelled snapshot, send it to GitHub.
phase1.example:
git add .
git commit -m "feat: hello world"
git push
phase1.def: git add stages changes for the next commit, git commit records a snapshot of the staged changes with a message, and git push uploads local commits to a remote repository.
phase1.model: Choose what goes in the photo, take the photo with a caption, then post it to the shared album.
phase1.game: After the runner's restart works: add the files, commit "feat: restart from game over", push so your partner can play it.
phase1.gameCode:
git add .
git commit -m "feat: restart from game over"
git push

phase1.what: Notes in the code that the compiler skips. // runs to the end of the line; /* */ can span lines.
phase1.example: int lives = 3;   // three, so one mistake isn't game over
phase1.gotcha: /* */ doesn't nest: the first */ ends the comment.
phase1.def: Comments are removed before the code is translated. A // comment ends at the end of its line (C99 and later); a /* */ comment ends at the first */ and cannot be nested.
phase1.model: Sticky notes on a recipe card. The cook reads round them.
phase1.game: Commenting out a line is the quickest way to switch something off while you test, like skipping the enemy spawn to check that the player moves.

phase1.what: A named box in memory that holds one value. Declare it with a type, then store values with =.
phase1.gotcha: Reading one before storing a value gives garbage (MSVC C4700).
phase1.def: A variable is a named object with a type. A declaration introduces the name and type, assignment (=) stores a new value, and an initialiser gives the first value as part of the declaration.
phase1.model: A labelled box on a shelf. One number fits; putting a new one in throws the old one out.
phase1.game: Score, lives, level and the player's lane are all variables. Every frame the game changes some of them and draws them all.

phase1.what: A name you choose: letters, digits and _, not starting with a digit, and not a keyword.
phase1.gotcha: Case-sensitive: Score and score are different names.
phase1.def: An identifier names a variable, function or type. It may contain letters, digits and underscores, must not begin with a digit, and must not be a keyword. Names beginning with an underscore are reserved for the implementation in many cases.
phase1.model: The label on the box. Write it clearly, because you'll read it hundreds of times.
phase1.game: Good names make game code read like the design: lives, enemy_count, player_lane. Names like x, n2 or tmp make every bug harder to find.

phase2.what: Whole numbers, about ±2.1 billion. Health, score, frame count.
phase2.def: int is the basic signed integer type. On MSVC for x86/x64 it is 32 bits, ranging from −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647.
phase2.model: A box that only holds whole numbers. No fractions get in.
phase2.game: Score, frame count, guess count, lives: things you count are ints.

phase2.what: Decimal numbers, ~7 digits. Positions, speed, timers. Write the f suffix.
phase2.def: float is a single-precision binary floating-point type, about 7 significant decimal digits. A literal with an f suffix (2.5f) has type float.
phase2.model: A box for measurements, not counts. Precise enough for positions on a screen, not for money.
phase2.game: In the window version, the player's x and y and its speed are floats so it can move 2.7 pixels a frame without losing the .7.

phase2.what: Decimal with ~15 digits. Read with %lf in scanf.
phase2.def: double is a double-precision floating-point type, about 15–16 significant digits. Unsuffixed decimal literals like 1.8 are doubles.
phase2.model: A float with a longer ruler. More digits, twice the memory.
phase2.game: You'll rarely need it in this game. It mostly shows up by accident: writing 1.8 instead of 1.8f makes a double and triggers C4305.

phase2.what: One byte holding a character's ASCII number. Single quotes.
phase2.def: char is the smallest addressable integer type, one byte. A character literal like 'A' is that character's code (65 in ASCII).
phase2.model: A number wearing a letter costume. %c shows the costume, %d shows the number.
phase2.game: The runner's lane is a row of chars: '.' for road, '#' for an obstacle, 'A' for the player, 'c' when ducking.

phase2.what: true or false. Needs #include <stdbool.h>. Prints as 1 or 0 with %d.
phase2.def: bool, from <stdbool.h>, is a type whose values are true (1) and false (0). In C99+, it's a macro for the built-in _Bool type.
phase2.model: A light switch: on or off, nothing in between.
phase2.game: Player.alive is a bool. When health hits 0, alive becomes false and the game moves to GAME_OVER.

phase2.what: printf/scanf slots: float, char, float to 2 places, string. Must match the type.
phase2.def: Conversion specifications tell printf/scanf the type of each argument: %f for float/double (printf), %c for a char, %s for a string, and precision like %.2f for decimal places.
phase2.model: Differently shaped slots on the form. A string won't fit in a %d slot, and forcing it prints nonsense.
phase2.game: The window debug readout shows position with %.1f and the player's name with %s.

phase2.what: Reads typed input into variables. Waits for Enter.
phase2.gotcha: The space before %c skips the leftover Enter. Returns how many values it read.
phase2.def: scanf reads formatted input from standard input according to a format string, storing results through pointer arguments. It returns the number of items successfully assigned.
phase2.model: A clerk who waits at the counter until you press Enter, then files what you typed into the boxes you pointed at.
phase2.game: The guessing game reads each guess with scanf. Phase 4.5 replaces it, because a game can't stop and wait for Enter.

phase2.what: The address of a variable, so a function can write into it.
phase2.def: The unary & operator yields the address of its operand — a pointer to it.
phase2.model: Writing down where a box lives instead of what's in it, so someone else can come and fill it.
phase2.game: scanf needs &guess because it has to put your number into the guess box in main, not into a copy.

phase2.what: int / int drops the fraction (7 / 2 is 3). % gives the remainder (7 % 2 is 1).
phase2.def: Dividing two integer operands performs integer division, truncating toward zero. % yields the remainder, with (a/b)*b + a%b == a.
phase2.model: Sharing sweets: 7 between 2 people is 3 each, 1 left over. / is the 3, % is the 1.
phase2.game: A health bar drawn as hp / max_hp is 0 until full. Multiply first: hp * 100 / max_hp gives a real percentage.
phase2.gameCode: int pct = hp * 100 / max_hp;   // not hp / max_hp * 100

phase2.what: Converts a value on purpose. float → int truncates toward zero.
phase2.def: A cast expression (type)expr converts a value to the named type. Converting a floating value to an integer type truncates toward zero.
phase2.model: Telling the compiler "I know this loses information, and I mean it".
phase2.game: To draw a float x position into the char lane, cast it to an int column. Do it once, at draw time, and never store it back.

phase2.what: Size in bytes, worked out by the compiler. Returns size_t: print with %zu (or cast to int for %d).
phase2.def: sizeof yields the size in bytes of a type or object, as a value of type size_t, computed at compile time for non-VLA operands.
phase2.model: Measuring the box, not looking inside it.
phase2.game: count = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]) tells the high-score table how many slots it has without typing 5 again.

phase2.what: Change a variable using its own value: score += 5 is score = score + 5.
phase2.gotcha: =+ is not +=. score =+ 5 just sets score to 5.
phase2.def: A compound assignment E1 op= E2 is equivalent to E1 = E1 op (E2), except that E1 is evaluated only once. The right operand is fully evaluated first.
phase2.model: Reach into the box, change what's there, put it back, all in one move.
phase2.game: Almost every update line in the game: moving the player, spending ammo, adding score.

phase2.what: Add or take away 1. Prefix (++x) changes then gives the new value; postfix (x++) gives the old value then changes.
phase2.gotcha: On a line of its own, x++ and ++x do the same thing.
phase2.def: The increment and decrement operators add or subtract 1 from an lvalue. The prefix form yields the updated value; the postfix form yields the value before the update.
phase2.model: A tally clicker. Postfix tells you the count, then clicks. Prefix clicks, then tells you.
phase2.game: The frame counter ticks with frame++ once per pass through the game loop.

phase2.what: A change an expression makes as well as producing a value: =, +=, ++ and -- all have one.
phase2.gotcha: Never change a variable and read it again in the same expression.
phase2.def: A side effect is a change in the state of the program, such as modifying an object, that happens as part of evaluating an expression. Modifying an object twice, or modifying and separately reading it, without a sequence point between is undefined.
phase2.model: Asking a question that also moves the furniture. Fine once; confusing if you ask two at the same time.
phase2.game: printf("%d %d", lives, lives--) has no right answer. Split it: print first, then lives--.

phase2.what: Something that can sit on the left of =: a box that can hold a value, like a variable.
phase2.def: An lvalue is an expression that designates an object, so it can be assigned to. Constants and the results of most operators are not lvalues.
phase2.model: A box with an address. A number on its own is just a value; there's nowhere to put anything.
phase2.game: player.x, lives and score[2] are all lvalues. lives - 1 isn't: store it with lives -= 1.

phase2.what: Which operator goes first: casts and ++, then * / %, then + -, then =. Same rank runs left to right.
phase2.gotcha: 100 / 10 * 2 is 20, not 5. Brackets when in doubt.
phase2.def: Precedence decides how operators group with their operands when there are no brackets; associativity decides grouping between operators of equal precedence (left to right for arithmetic, right to left for assignment).
phase2.model: The order of operations from school maths, with a few extra rungs for C's own operators.
phase2.game: A damage formula that forgets its brackets subtracts armour from the wrong thing.

phase2.what: Code the C standard makes no promise about. It may work, print rubbish or crash. Treat it as a bug.
phase2.gotcha: Seeming to work is not proof. It can break when you change something unrelated.
phase2.def: Behaviour for which the C standard imposes no requirements, such as signed integer overflow, integer division by zero, or modifying an object twice between sequence points. Implementation-defined behaviour, by contrast, is documented and consistent for a given compiler.
phase2.model: Walking off the edge of the map. The game might not crash right away, but nothing out there is promised.
phase2.game: A score that overflows an int is undefined. Give it a type with room instead of hoping it wraps.

phase2.what: A number growing past what its type can hold. Unsigned wraps round; signed is undefined behaviour.
phase2.gotcha: On Windows long is 4 bytes, so it overflows at the same point as int. Use long long.
phase2.def: Overflow occurs when an arithmetic result is outside the range of its type. Unsigned arithmetic is reduced modulo 2^N (it wraps); signed integer overflow is undefined behaviour.
phase2.model: A mileage counter with a fixed number of wheels. Roll past the end and the number is no longer the real one.
phase2.game: An int frame counter at 60 fps lasts about 414 days. A lifetime XP total may need a long long.

phase2.what: A whole number with no negatives and twice the positive range. Print with %u.
phase2.gotcha: Mixed with an int, the int turns unsigned: 3u - 5 is 4294967294.
phase2.def: unsigned integer types represent only non-negative values. unsigned int on MSVC is 32 bits, 0 to 4,294,967,295. When a signed and an unsigned int meet, the signed one is converted to unsigned.
phase2.model: A counter that starts at 0 and can't go below it. Push it down past 0 and it reappears at the top.
phase2.game: Keep scores and lives as int. unsigned is for sizes, colours and bit flags, and for srand's seed.

phase2b.what: Runs the first block whose condition is true; the rest are skipped.
phase2b.def: if evaluates a controlling expression and executes its statement when the result is non-zero; else if and else chain alternatives that are tested in order.
phase2b.model: A row of gates. You go through the first one that's open and skip all the rest.
phase2b.game: The guessing game's whole personality: too high, too low, or correct — exactly one message per guess.

phase2b.what: == compares and gives 1 or 0. = assigns and gives the assigned value.
phase2b.gotcha: /W4 warns with C4706 inside a condition.
phase2b.def: == is the equality operator and yields 1 or 0. = is the assignment operator; the expression's value is the value assigned.
phase2b.model: == asks a question. = gives an order. Mixing them up asks nothing and quietly changes your data.
phase2b.game: if (health = 0) sets health to zero and never runs the block — the player can't die and also has no health.

phase2b.what: Repeat while the condition is true. For loops that wait for something to change.
phase2b.def: while repeatedly executes its body as long as its controlling expression evaluates to non-zero, testing before each iteration.
phase2b.model: "Keep going until something changes." You don't know how many times; you know what makes it stop.
phase2b.game: The frame loop is a while: keep drawing frames until the player quits.

phase2b.what: Repeat a known number of times: start; keep going while; step.
phase2b.def: for combines initialisation, a controlling expression tested before each iteration, and an expression evaluated after each iteration.
phase2b.model: "Do this exactly N times", with the counter's whole life written on one line.
phase2b.game: Every frame the runner walks all 8 obstacle slots with the same for header.
phase2b.gameCode: for (i = 0; i < MAX_OBS; i++) { /* move obs[i] */ }

phase2b.what: A loop that always runs at least once. Good for "play, then ask again".
phase2b.def: do-while executes its body, then tests the controlling expression, so the body always runs at least once.
phase2b.model: Try first, ask after. You always get one go.
phase2b.game: Guess v2's "Play again? (y/n)" — play one round, then ask whether to loop.

phase2b.what: Picks a branch by value. Cleaner than many ifs for menus and states.
phase2b.gotcha: Forget break and it falls into the next case.
phase2b.def: switch transfers control to the case label whose constant matches the controlling expression's value, or to default. Execution falls through to the next case unless a break intervenes.
phase2b.model: A railway junction: the value picks the track, and break is where you get off.
phase2b.game: The runner's state machine is one switch on state: MENU, PLAYING, GAME_OVER.

phase2b.what: rand() gives a pseudo-random number; seed it once with srand(time(NULL)).
phase2b.def: rand returns a pseudo-random int in [0, RAND_MAX]; srand seeds the sequence. Seeding with time(NULL) gives a different sequence each run.
phase2b.model: A recipe that turns one number into the next forever. srand picks where in the recipe you start.
phase2b.game: The guessing game's secret number, and later, how far apart the runner's obstacles spawn.

phase2b.what: And, or, not. Join comparisons; the answer is always 1 or 0.
phase2b.gotcha: 0 < x < 10 is always true. Write x > 0 && x < 10.
phase2b.def: && yields 1 if both operands are non-zero, || yields 1 if either is non-zero, and ! yields 1 if its operand is 0. All three yield an int, 1 or 0. && binds more tightly than ||.
phase2b.model: Gates. && opens only for two yeses, || opens for one, ! swaps yes and no.
phase2b.game: The runner's collision test is one && chain: same lane and same column means a hit.

phase2b.what: && stops at the first false side, || at the first true one. The rest never runs.
phase2b.gotcha: A ++ on the right side may never happen.
phase2b.def: The left operand of && and || is evaluated first; the right operand is evaluated only if the result isn't already decided.
phase2b.model: A bouncer who checks your ID first. No ID, and nobody bothers asking your name.
phase2b.game: Guard a division or an array slot with a test on the left, so the risky part only runs when it's safe.
phase2b.gameCode: if (count > 0 && total / count > best) best = total / count;

phase2b.what: test ? a : b picks a value: a when the test is true, b when it isn't.
phase2b.gotcha: Binds very loosely: bracket it inside bigger sums.
phase2b.def: The conditional operator evaluates its first operand; if non-zero the result is the second operand, otherwise the third. Only one of the two is evaluated.
phase2b.model: An if that hands back a value instead of running a block.
phase2b.game: The runner draws the player as 'c' when ducking and 'A' otherwise, in one line.

phase2b.what: break leaves the innermost loop or switch; continue jumps to the next lap.
phase2b.gotcha: break inside a switch inside a loop only leaves the switch.
phase2b.def: break jumps out of the nearest loop or switch it sits in, and only that one. continue ends the current iteration of the innermost loop; in a for, the step expression runs next. for (;;) has no controlling expression and loops until something inside leaves it.
phase2b.model: Side doors on a lap: continue goes back to the start line, break leaves the track.
phase2b.game: The runner's obstacle spawner walks the slots and breaks out at the first free one.
phase2b.gameCode:
for (i = 0; i < MAX_OBS; i++)
    if (obs[i] == -1) { obs[i] = LANE_LEN - 1; break; }

phase2b.what: Reads one character, as an int so it can also return EOF.
phase2b.gotcha: Store the result in an int, not a char, or EOF can be missed.
phase2b.def: getchar reads the next character from standard input and returns it as an unsigned char converted to int, or EOF at end of input or on error.
phase2b.model: Taking one letter at a time off the front of the queue of everything typed.
phase2b.game: After a bad scanf, a getchar loop throws away the rest of the line so the next read starts clean.
phase2b.gameCode:
int c;
while ((c = getchar()) != '\n' && c != EOF) { }

phase3.what: A named machine: inputs (parameters) in, one result (return value) out.
phase3.def: A function is a named block of code with parameters and an optional return value, defined once and called from elsewhere.
phase3.model: A vending machine: put something in, it does one job, and something (or nothing) comes out.
phase3.game: clamp_health keeps health between 0 and 100, so every place that changes health uses the same rule.

phase3.what: "Nothing": a function that returns no value, or takes no parameters.
phase3.def: void denotes the absence of a value: as a return type, the function returns nothing; as a parameter list (void), it takes no arguments.
phase3.model: A machine with no output tray. It does something (prints, moves) but hands nothing back.
phase3.game: print_banner draws the title screen and returns nothing.
phase3.gameCode: void print_banner(void) { printf("ASCII RUNNER\n"); }

phase3.what: A one-line promise that a function exists, so it can be called before its body.
phase3.def: A function prototype is a declaration giving a function's name, return type and parameter types, letting calls be checked before the definition appears.
phase3.model: A promise on the first page of a book: "chapter 9 explains this", so you can mention it in chapter 2.
phase3.game: With prototypes at the top, main can sit first in high_score.c and call insert_score defined further down.
phase3.gameCode: void insert_score(int scores[], int count, int new_score);

phase3.what: Find-and-replace before compiling. Name your magic numbers.
phase3.def: #define creates a preprocessor macro: every later occurrence of the name is textually replaced before compilation.
phase3.model: Find-and-replace on your file before the compiler reads it.
phase3.game: MAX_SCORES, LANE_LEN, MAX_OBS: change one line and every array and loop that uses it follows.
phase3.gameCode:
#define MAX_OBS 8
int obs[MAX_OBS];

phase3.what: A row of same-type boxes reached by index, starting at 0.
phase3.gotcha: Last index is size - 1; C won't stop you going past it.
phase3.def: An array is a contiguous sequence of elements of one type, accessed by an integer index starting at 0. C performs no bounds checking.
phase3.model: A row of numbered lockers, all the same size. Locker 0 is the first one.
phase3.game: obs[8] holds the column of every obstacle; -1 means the slot is empty.
phase3.gameCode:
int obs[MAX_OBS];
obs[0] = LANE_LEN - 1;   // spawn at the far right

phase3.what: The one loop shape for arrays. Never <= count.
phase3.def: The canonical array traversal initialises the index to 0 and continues while it is less than the element count, so it visits indices 0 to count − 1.
phase3.model: Visit every locker, starting at 0, and stop before the number that doesn't exist.
phase3.game: The same header moves obstacles, draws them and checks collisions: three loops, one shape.
phase3.gameCode:
for (i = 0; i < MAX_OBS; i++)
    if (obs[i] >= 0) obs[i]--;

phase3.what: How many elements an array has, where it was declared.
phase3.gotcha: Inside a function you only have where the array lives, not the array; pass the count.
phase3.def: Dividing the size of an array by the size of one element yields its element count, valid only where the array's declaration (not a pointer) is in scope.
phase3.model: The length of the whole locker row divided by the width of one locker.
phase3.game: Useful in main for the starting high-score table, but pass the count into functions, because they only get the array's location.
phase3.gameCode: int count = (int)(sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]));

phase3.what: A char array that ends at the first '\0'. %s prints up to it.
phase3.def: A C string is a contiguous sequence of chars terminated by the first null character ('\0'). String functions and %s process characters up to that terminator.
phase3.model: A row of letter tiles with a stop sign at the end. Everything after the stop sign is ignored.
phase3.game: The runner's lane is a string: 50 tiles of road and obstacles, then a '\0' so printf knows where the track ends.
phase3.gameCode:
char lane[LANE_LEN + 1];
lane[LANE_LEN] = '\0';

phase3.what: The terminator byte, value 0. Not the digit '0' (48).
phase3.def: '\0' is the null character, with value 0. It marks the end of a C string. It differs from the digit '0', which has value 48.
phase3.model: The stop sign at the end of the word.
phase3.game: Forget it at the end of the lane and printf keeps going into whatever memory comes next: a screen of junk after your track.
phase3.gameCode: lane[LANE_LEN] = '\0';

phase3.what: Reads a whole line safely: never writes past the size you give it.
phase3.gotcha: Keeps the Enter as '\n'. Strip it.
phase3.def: fgets reads at most n−1 characters from a stream into a buffer, stopping after a newline, and always null-terminates. It returns NULL on failure or end of file.
phase3.model: A form with a fixed number of boxes. You can't write past the last box, and Enter gets written in too.
phase3.game: Reading the player's name for the high-score table, then chopping off the Enter.
phase3.gameCode:
fgets(name, NAME_LEN, stdin);
name[strcspn(name, "\n")] = '\0';

phase3.what: Counts characters up to the '\0', not including it. Returns size_t.
phase3.def: strlen returns the number of characters before the terminating null character, as a size_t.
phase3.model: Counting tiles up to the stop sign, not counting the sign.
phase3.game: Centering a name on the game-over screen needs its length.
phase3.gameCode: int pad = (LANE_LEN - (int)strlen(name)) / 2;

phase3.what: Compares two strings. 0 means equal; only the sign of other results is guaranteed.
phase3.gotcha: if (strcmp(a, b)) runs when they're different.
phase3.def: strcmp compares two strings lexicographically, returning zero if equal, and a negative or positive value if the first sorts before or after the second.
phase3.model: It answers “how do these two sort?”, not “are these the same?”, and 0 means they’re identical.
phase3.game: Checking whether a new high score belongs to a name already on the table.
phase3.gameCode: if (strcmp(names[i], name) == 0) { /* same player */ }

phase3.what: An array of arrays, such as five names of up to 31 characters.
phase3.def: A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays; names[5][32] is five arrays of 32 chars, stored row after row.
phase3.model: A shelf of five name tags, each with room for 31 letters.
phase3.game: The high-score table keeps names[MAX_SCORES][NAME_LEN] in step with scores[MAX_SCORES].
phase3.gameCode:
char names[MAX_SCORES][NAME_LEN];
snprintf(names[0], NAME_LEN, "%s", "SAM");

phase3.what: A variable declared inside { } only exists inside them, and is gone when the function returns.
phase3.example: void f(void) { int x = 1; }   // x is gone after this
phase3.def: A variable declared in a block has block scope and, unless static, automatic storage: it exists from its declaration until the block ends.
phase3.model: Notes on a whiteboard in a meeting room. When the meeting ends, the board is wiped.
phase3.game: The lane buffer in runner_render is local: rebuilt every frame, gone when the function returns. Score lives in the Runner struct because it must survive.

phase3.what: Open a file, write or read it like printf/scanf, then close it.
phase3.gotcha: fopen returns NULL if it can't open. MSVC needs _CRT_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS.
phase3.def: fopen opens a file and returns a FILE pointer (or NULL); fprintf and fscanf write and read formatted text through it; fclose flushes and closes it.
phase3.model: Opening a notebook, writing in it like you'd print to the screen, and closing it so the ink dries.
phase3.game: Saving the best score to best.txt so the runner's menu can show "Best: 41" next time.
phase3.gameCode:
FILE* f = fopen("best.txt", "w");
if (f) { fprintf(f, "%d\n", best); fclose(f); }

phase3.what: A local variable that keeps its value between calls. Made once, before main starts.
phase3.gotcha: The = 0 runs once. It does not reset the value on each call.
phase3.def: A block-scope variable declared static has static storage duration: it exists for the whole run and is initialised once, before program start-up (to zero if no initialiser is given). Its scope is unchanged: the name is visible only inside its block.
phase3.model: A tally sheet in a meeting room's locked drawer. It's still there next meeting, and only that room has the key.
phase3.game: A function that hands out a new ID for each enemy can keep its next-ID counter as a static local, so no other code can mess with it.

phase3.what: A variable declared outside every function. Every function below it can read and change it.
phase3.example:
int wave = 1;   // above every function

void spawn_enemy(void) { printf("%d", wave); }
phase3.gotcha: Any function can change it, so a wrong value could come from anywhere. A local with the same name is C4459.
phase3.def: A variable declared at file scope has static storage duration (it exists for the whole run and starts at zero if not initialised) and is visible from its declaration to the end of the file.
phase3.model: The scoreboard in the corridor. Everyone can read it, and anyone can change it.
phase3.game: The Win32 starters keep a running flag as a global, because Windows calls the window procedure directly and you can't pass it extra arguments.
phase3.gameCode: int running = 1;   // read by the game loop, cleared by WndProc

phase3.what: A function takes an array as int a[] plus a count, and works on the caller's real array.
phase3.example:
void add_bonus(int scores[], int count, int bonus);
add_bonus(scores, count, 5);
phase3.gotcha: sizeof inside the function gives the size of a location (8 bytes on x64), not the array, and MSVC doesn't warn. Always pass the count.
phase3.def: A parameter declared as an array of T is adjusted to a pointer to T (pointers are Phase 3.5). The argument is the address of the array's first element, so the function accesses the caller's elements directly, and any length written in the brackets is ignored.
phase3.model: Lending the key to your row of lockers, not photocopying what's inside.
phase3.game: The high-score table's insert_score takes the scores array and its count, and shifts the caller's scores down in place.
phase3.gameCode: void insert_score(int scores[], int count, int new_score);

phase3.what: The three streams every program starts with: keyboard in, screen out, and a separate screen route for errors.
phase3.example:
fgets(line, sizeof(line), stdin);
fprintf(stderr, "Could not save\n");
phase3.gotcha: > file.txt redirects stdout only. Errors on stderr still reach the screen.
phase3.def: stdin, stdout and stderr are FILE streams opened before main runs: standard input, standard output and standard error. stderr is not fully buffered, so its output appears promptly.
phase3.model: Three pipes already plumbed in: one bringing typing in, one carrying normal output, and an emergency line for problems.
phase3.game: The save code reports a failed fopen on stderr, so the message shows even when normal output goes to a log.

phase3.what: scanf that reads from a string instead of the keyboard. Pair it with fgets to read numbers.
phase3.gotcha: MSVC flags it C4996, like scanf.
phase3.def: sscanf parses formatted input from a string using the same conversion specifications as scanf, and returns the number of items assigned, or EOF if input ends before the first conversion.
phase3.model: Reading the answer off a note the player already handed you, instead of listening to them type.
phase3.game: The lane prompt reads a whole line with fgets, then sscanf pulls the number out, so stray letters never jam the next read.
phase3.gameCode:
char line[16];
if (fgets(line, sizeof(line), stdin) && sscanf(line, "%d", &lane) == 1) { }

phase3.what: printf into a char array, never past the size you give. The safe way to copy and join text.
phase3.gotcha: Returns the length it wanted. A result >= size means the text was cut.
phase3.def: snprintf writes formatted output to a buffer, storing at most size - 1 characters plus a terminating null (when size is not 0). It returns the number of characters the full output would have contained, or a negative value on an encoding error.
phase3.model: printf with a box count: it writes what fits, always leaves room for the stop sign, and tells you how much it wanted.
phase3.game: Building the score line for the screen from a name and a number, cut safely if the name is too long.
phase3.gameCode:
char line[32];
snprintf(line, sizeof(line), "%s: %d", name, score);

phase3.what: Copy a string into an array. strcpy has no size check; strncpy can leave no '\0'.
phase3.gotcha: MSVC flags both C4996. For text from outside, use snprintf.
phase3.def: strcpy copies a string, including its terminator, into a destination array; strncpy copies at most n characters and does not add a terminator if the source is n characters or longer. Neither checks the destination's size.
phase3.model: Pouring from one jug into another without looking at the second jug's size.
phase3.game: Shifting the names table down a row when a new high score comes in: every row is the same size, so each copy fits.
phase3.gameCode:
for (i = MAX_SCORES - 1; i > slot; i--)
    strcpy(names[i], names[i - 1]);

phase3.what: Add one string onto the end of another. strcat has no size check.
phase3.gotcha: strncat's n is the space left minus 1, not sizeof(msg).
phase3.def: strcat appends a copy of the source string to the end of the destination string; strncat appends at most n characters and always writes a terminator. Neither knows the destination's total size.
phase3.model: Writing more words after the last one on a line, without checking how much line is left.
phase3.game: Joining "Player: " and a name for the HUD. snprintf does the same job with the size built in.
phase3.gameCode: snprintf(hud, sizeof(hud), "Player: %s", name);   // instead of strcat

phase3.what: From ctype.h: one letter to a capital (or small letter). Anything else comes back unchanged.
phase3.gotcha: Cast to unsigned char first: MSVC's char is signed.
phase3.def: toupper and tolower, declared in <ctype.h>, convert a lowercase letter to uppercase or the reverse. The argument must be representable as unsigned char or be EOF; other values are undefined.
phase3.model: A stamp that only works on letters: press it on a digit or a space and nothing changes.
phase3.game: Accepting q, Q, quit or QUIT at the menu by uppercasing what the player typed before comparing.
phase3.gameCode:
for (i = 0; cmd[i] != '\0'; i++)
    cmd[i] = (char)toupper((unsigned char)cmd[i]);

phase3b.what: Groups named fields of different types into one type.
phase3b.def: A struct type groups named members, possibly of different types, into one object. typedef gives the type a single-word name.
phase3b.model: A form with labelled boxes: name, position, health, everything about one thing, kept together.
phase3b.game: The Runner struct holds the whole game's state, so functions take one pointer instead of six variables.

phase3b.what: The dot reaches a field when you hold the struct itself.
phase3b.def: The . operator accesses a member of a struct object you hold directly.
phase3b.model: Reaching into a box you're holding and taking out one labelled item.
phase3b.game: In main you hold the Runner itself, so it's r.score.

phase3b.what: b = a copies every field. Passing a struct to a function copies it too.
phase3b.example: Player b = a;   // two separate players
phase3b.def: Structs have value semantics: assignment and pass-by-value copy every member into a separate object.
phase3b.model: Photocopying the whole form. Scribbling on the copy doesn't change the original.
phase3b.game: runner_update(Runner r, …) without the * updates a photocopy every frame. Nothing ever moves on screen.
phase3b.gameCode: void runner_update(Runner r, int key);   // copy, changes are lost

phase3b.what: A variable that holds an address, where a value lives, not the value.
phase3b.def: A pointer is an object whose value is the address of another object of a given type.
phase3b.model: A note with a house address written on it. It's not the house; it tells you where the house is.
phase3b.game: Runner* r inside runner_update points at the one real Runner in main.

phase3b.what: Dereference: go to the address in p and use what's there.
phase3b.def: The unary * operator applied to a pointer yields the object it points to.
phase3b.model: Going to the address on the note and opening the front door.
phase3b.game: (*r).score is the real score in main's Runner, same as r->score.

phase3b.what: Address-of: the location of x. Hand it to functions that should change x.
phase3b.def: The unary & operator yields the address of its operand.
phase3b.model: Writing down the address of a house so someone else can visit it.
phase3b.game: main hands runner_update the address of its Runner, so the update reaches the real game.

phase3b.what: Field through a pointer. Shorthand for (*p).health.
phase3b.def: p->m is shorthand for (*p).m: the member m of the struct that pointer p points to.
phase3b.model: Follow the address, then grab the labelled item, in one move.
phase3b.game: Every line of runner.c that touches the game reads r->something.

phase3b.what: Functions that change an object take a pointer, so they change the real one.
phase3b.example: void player_move(Player* p, float dx, float dy);
phase3b.def: Passing a pointer gives the called function access to the caller's object, so modifications persist after it returns.
phase3b.model: Giving someone your address instead of a photocopy of your house plans.
phase3b.game: player_take_damage(&hero, 10) lowers the real hero's health.

phase3b.what: A pointer to nothing. Check for it before using a pointer.
phase3b.def: NULL is a null pointer constant: a pointer value guaranteed not to point to any object.
phase3b.model: A blank note, no address written on it. Going there gets you nowhere, fast.
phase3b.game: fopen returns NULL when best.txt doesn't exist yet. Check before reading, or the first run crashes.
phase3b.gameCode:
FILE* f = fopen("best.txt", "r");
if (f == NULL) best = 0;

phase3b.what: Set struct fields by name as you create it. Fields you leave out become 0.
phase3b.gotcha: Any field you don't name is 0, not garbage.
phase3b.def: A designated initialiser names the member it initialises (.member = value), so members can be given in any order. Members not named are initialised to zero. Standard since C99.
phase3b.model: Filling in a form by label instead of by position: you write health next to “health”, wherever it sits on the page.
phase3b.game: A new enemy only needs the fields that matter; everything else starts at 0.

phase3b.what: An array where every box is a whole struct. Index first, then the dot: enemies[i].health.
phase3b.gotcha: Loop to count, not MAX_ENEMIES. A search returns -1 for not found: check it before using it as an index.
phase3b.def: An array whose element type is a structure. Each element is a complete struct object, accessed by index, and its members are accessed with the . operator.
phase3b.model: A row of lockers, each holding a whole form. The index picks the locker, the dot picks the box on the form.
phase3b.game: Phase 6's enemies, bullets and pickups are each one array of structs plus a count, updated by one loop every frame.

phase3b.what: p + 1 is the next element, not the next byte. Subtracting two pointers gives how many elements apart they are.
phase3b.gotcha: Pointing one past the end is legal; reading there is not.
phase3b.def: When a pointer points into an array, adding n to it gives a pointer n elements further along, with the step scaled by the size of the element type. The difference of two pointers into the same array is the number of elements between them.
phase3b.model: A finger pointing at a locker. p + 2 is two lockers along, whatever size the lockers are.
phase3b.game: A pointer loop over the obstacle array stops at obs + count, one past the last obstacle.

phase3b.what: In an expression, an array's name turns into a pointer to its first element. So a[i] is *(a + i), and int a[] as a parameter is int* a.
phase3b.gotcha: sizeof(array) is the whole array; sizeof(pointer) is 8 on x64. You can't assign to an array name.
phase3b.def: Apart from sizeof and unary &, using an array in an expression converts it to a pointer to element 0. A parameter declared as an array of T is adjusted to pointer to T.
phase3b.model: Handing someone the key to the first locker instead of the whole row. They can reach every locker from there, but they can't tell how many there are.
phase3b.game: runner_draw(lane, LANE_LEN) passes the lane's address, which is why the function needs the length as well.
phase3b.gameCode: void runner_draw(const char* lane, int len);

phase3b.what: A pointer to text you read but don't change, like a string in quotes.
phase3b.gotcha: Text in quotes may be read-only. Need to change it? Copy it into char name[].
phase3b.def: A pointer to const char. String literals have static storage and must not be modified; pointing at them through const char* makes the compiler reject writes.
phase3b.model: A pointer to a sign on the wall: you can read it as often as you like, but you can't repaint it.
phase3b.game: A table of enemy kinds keeps each fixed name as a const char*.
phase3b.gameCode:
typedef struct { const char* name; int health; } EnemyKind;
const EnemyKind KINDS[2] = {{"Slime", 30}, {"Bat", 20}};

phase3c.what: .h declares what exists (types, prototypes). .c holds the bodies.
phase3c.example:
// player.h
void player_heal(Player* p, int amount);
phase3c.def: Headers (.h) hold declarations shared between translation units; source files (.c) hold definitions that are compiled once.
phase3c.model: The menu on the restaurant door (.h) versus the kitchen (.c).
phase3c.game: runner.h lists what the runner can do; runner.c does it; main.c only needs the menu.

phase3c.what: Top of a header: include this file only once per .c file.
phase3c.gotcha: Without it, a double include defines the typedef twice: C2371.
phase3c.def: #pragma once is a widely supported directive asking the compiler to include the current file at most once per translation unit.
phase3c.model: A "you've already read this page" bookmark.
phase3c.game: main.c and runner.c can both include runner.h without the Runner struct being defined twice.

phase3c.what: The compiler was happy but the body was never built, a .c file is missing from the build.
phase3c.example: cl main.c player.c   // list every .c file
phase3c.def: The linker resolves each referenced symbol to exactly one definition across all object files. LNK2019 means a referenced symbol has no definition.
phase3c.model: The compiler checked every promise; the linker goes to collect, and one chapter is missing from the book.
phase3c.game: Take runner.c out of the SOURCES line: main.c still compiles, but runner_update has no body to link to.

phase3c.what: Breakpoint · run/continue · step over · step into. Watch panel shows live values.
phase3c.example: F9 on a line, F5, then F10 to step
phase3c.gotcha: Run build first, F5 launches the exe on disk.
phase3c.def: A debugger pauses a running program at breakpoints and lets you step line by line and inspect variables, using debug symbols from the PDB.
phase3c.model: A pause button for your program, plus X-ray vision into every box.
phase3c.game: Breakpoint on the hit test in runner_update, then watch r->obs and ducking to see exactly why you died.

phase3c.what: Named integer constants, perfect for game states.
phase3c.def: An enumeration defines a set of named integer constants; typedef enum gives the set a type name.
phase3c.model: Named positions on a dial instead of numbers you have to remember.
phase3c.game: GameState gives the runner three readable states, and the switch reads like a sentence.
phase3c.gameCode: typedef enum { STATE_MENU, STATE_PLAYING, STATE_GAME_OVER } GameState;

phase3c.what: A variable that holds a function's address. Call through it like the function itself.
phase3c.gotcha: update_menu is the address; update_menu() is a call. Calling a NULL one crashes.
phase3c.def: A pointer to a function stores the address of a function of a particular type; calling through it invokes that function. A function designator used without a call is converted to a pointer to the function.
phase3c.model: A speed-dial slot: it holds a number to ring, not the person.
phase3c.game: A table of update functions indexed by GameState, so one line runs the right code for the menu, play or game over.
phase3c.gameCode:
UpdateFn updates[STATE_COUNT] = { update_menu, update_playing, NULL };
state = updates[state](frame);

phase3c.what: The standard way to stop a header being pasted twice into one .c file.
phase3c.gotcha: Every header needs its own guard name. Two headers using the same name hide each other.
phase3c.def: An include guard wraps a header in #ifndef NAME / #define NAME / #endif, so its contents are processed only the first time it is included in a translation unit.
phase3c.model: A sign on the door: if this name is already on the list, skip the room.
phase3c.game: enemy.h includes player.h, and so does main.c. The guard keeps Player defined once.

phase3c.what: Declares a global that is defined in another .c file. Goes in the header.
phase3c.gotcha: The definition (with or without = value) goes in exactly one .c file, never in the header.
phase3c.def: extern declares an identifier with external linkage without defining it, so code in one file can refer to an object defined in another.
phase3c.model: A forwarding note: "the real high score is kept in game.c".
phase3c.game: main.c and hud.c both read high_score; only game.c owns it.

phase3c.what: On a function, or a variable outside every function: visible only inside this .c file.
phase3c.gotcha: Leave it out of the header. Another file that calls it gets a build error.
phase3c.def: At file scope, static gives a function or object internal linkage: its name is not visible to the linker from other translation units.
phase3c.model: A note pinned inside the kitchen: the cooks use it, the customers never see it.
phase3c.game: player.c keeps clamp_health to itself, so enemy.c can have its own clamp_health with no clash.
phase3c.gameCode: static int clamp_health(int h);   // in player.c, not player.h

phase4.what: Copy a repo to your machine; bring down your partner's new commits.
phase4.def: git clone copies a remote repository, with its full history, to your machine. git pull fetches new commits from the remote and merges them into your branch.
phase4.model: Photocopying the shared notebook once, then regularly copying in the new pages your partner wrote.
phase4.game: Your partner clones the game repo once, then pulls every session to get your latest runner changes.

phase4.what: A separate line of work. main stays buildable; features live on branches.
phase4.def: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit, letting a line of work evolve separately from main until it's merged.
phase4.model: A parallel draft of the story. Write freely; main stays readable.
phase4.game: feature/jump-obstacle lives on its own branch while main keeps a version of the runner that always builds.

phase4.what: Ask to merge a branch into main, with a review first.
phase4.def: A pull request asks to merge one branch into another, with a diff and a place for review comments before merging.
phase4.model: Handing your partner the draft and asking "read this before it goes in the book".
phase4.game: Open a PR for the jump obstacle; your partner plays it, comments, and merges.

phase4.what: Two changes to the same lines. Git marks both; you pick, delete the markers, commit.
phase4.def: A merge conflict occurs when two branches changed the same lines differently; Git marks both versions in the file for a person to resolve.
phase4.model: Two editors rewrote the same sentence. Someone has to pick the wording.
phase4.game: You both changed FRAME_MS. Pick one value, delete the markers, commit.

phase4.what: Files Git should never track: build output like .exe, .obj, .pdb.
phase4.def: .gitignore lists file patterns Git should not track, typically generated files like build output.
phase4.model: A "don't photocopy these" list taped to the notebook.
phase4.game: runner.exe, *.obj and *.pdb are rebuilt every time — keep them out so they never conflict.

phase4.what: type: short description — feat, fix, refactor, docs.
phase4.def: A commit message describes a change. A common convention is type: summary, with types such as feat, fix, refactor and docs.
phase4.model: The caption on the photo — what changed and why, readable by someone who wasn't there.
phase4.game: "fix: obstacle at column 0 no longer kills a ducking player" tells your partner exactly what to test.
phase4.gameCode: git commit -m "fix: ducking now dodges obstacles at column 0"

phase4b.what: Is a key waiting? (never waits) / take that key (no Enter, no echo).
phase4b.def: _kbhit (conio.h, Microsoft) returns non-zero if a keystroke is waiting in the console input buffer, without blocking. _getch reads one keystroke without echo or waiting for Enter.
phase4b.model: Glancing at the letterbox instead of waiting at the door. If there's post, take it; if not, carry on.
phase4b.game: The runner's input step: drain every key typed since last frame, keep the latest.

phase4b.what: Gives the CPU back for at least ms milliseconds. From <windows.h>.
phase4b.gotcha: At least, never exactly — about 15.6 ms granularity.
phase4b.def: Sleep (windows.h) suspends the calling thread for at least the given number of milliseconds; actual duration depends on the scheduler's timer resolution.
phase4b.model: Telling the CPU "wake me in about 33 ms" — about, not exactly.
phase4b.game: Sleep(FRAME_MS) holds the runner near 30 frames a second so obstacles don't fly past in a blur.

phase4b.what: Print a whole frame starting with \r and no \n: it paints over the last one.
phase4b.def: Printing a carriage return without a newline returns the cursor to the start of the current line, so the next output overwrites it.
phase4b.model: Rewinding the typewriter to the start of the line and typing over it.
phase4b.game: The runner's entire renderer: one line, repainted every frame, never scrolling.

phase4b.what: Push buffered output to the screen now. Needed when a line has no \n.
phase4b.def: fflush(stdout) writes any buffered output for standard output to the console immediately.
phase4b.model: Pushing the letter through the slot instead of waiting until the bag is full.
phase4b.game: The runner's frame has no \n, so without fflush it sits in the buffer and nothing appears.

phase4b.what: Build the whole frame in memory, then show it in one go. No flicker.
phase4b.def: A frame buffer is memory holding a complete frame that's built first and then presented in one operation.
phase4b.model: Painting the whole picture backstage, then rolling it out — instead of painting live in front of the audience.
phase4b.game: lane[] is the runner's frame buffer: fill it with road, stamp obstacles and the player, then print it once.

phase4b.what: An enum for the current state and one switch that does that state's work.
phase4b.def: A finite-state machine has a current state and transitions between states triggered by events; in C, typically an enum plus a switch.
phase4b.model: A board game's phases: setup, your turn, game over. Each phase has its own rules.
phase4b.game: MENU waits for a key, PLAYING moves and collides, GAME_OVER waits for R.

phase4b.what: A value meaning "empty", so a fixed array can be reused instead of allocating.
phase4b.def: A sentinel value is a reserved value meaning "empty" or "end", letting fixed-size storage represent varying amounts of data.
phase4b.model: An empty parking space marked with a cone instead of tearing up the space.
phase4b.game: obs[i] == -1 means slot i is free. Spawning finds a -1; dodging sets one back.
phase4b.gameCode:
for (i = 0; i < MAX_OBS; i++)
    if (obs[i] == -1) { obs[i] = LANE_LEN - 1; break; }

phase4b.what: The four steps every frame of every game.
phase4b.def: A game loop repeats every frame: gather input, update the simulation, render the result, then wait or measure until the next frame.
phase4b.model: The heartbeat of every game: look, think, draw, breathe.
phase4b.game: main.c after the split is exactly these four lines, forever.

phase4b.what: A read-only pointer: the function promises not to change what it points at.
phase4b.def: A pointer to const (const T* p) permits reading the pointed-to object but not modifying it through that pointer.
phase4b.model: A visitor's pass: you can look around the house, but you can't move the furniture.
phase4b.game: runner_render only draws. const Runner* r makes the compiler stop you if drawing accidentally changes the score.

phase4b.what: A body or variable in a header got included into two .c files.
phase4b.example:
// runner.h: declarations only
void runner_reset(Runner* r);
phase4b.def: LNK2005 means a symbol was defined in more than one object file — often because a header contains a definition and is included by several .c files.
phase4b.model: Two kitchens both claim to cook the same dish. The waiter doesn't know which to serve.
phase4b.game: int score = 0; in runner.h gives main.obj and runner.obj a score each.
phase4b.gameCode: // runner.h — declarations only, no bodies, no variables

phase5.what: The starting point of a Windows GUI program, instead of main.
phase5.example: int WINAPI WinMain(HINSTANCE h, HINSTANCE p, LPSTR cmd, int show)
phase5.def: WinMain is the conventional entry point for a Windows GUI application, receiving the instance handle, command line and initial show state.
phase5.model: main's Windows twin, with a few extra items handed over at the door.
phase5.game: The window prototype starts in WinMain, registers its window class, then runs the message loop.
phase5.gameCode: int WINAPI WinMain(HINSTANCE inst, HINSTANCE prev, LPSTR cmd, int show)

phase5.what: A handle — an ID number — for one window.
phase5.def: HWND is a handle — an opaque identifier — for a window managed by the operating system.
phase5.model: A cloakroom ticket. You don't hold the coat; you hold the number that gets it back.
phase5.game: Every drawing or redraw call for the prototype's window takes its HWND.

phase5.what: Collect Windows' messages (keys, clicks, close) and hand each to your WndProc.
phase5.def: A Win32 message loop retrieves messages from the thread's queue and dispatches them to the window procedure.
phase5.model: Checking your post and handing each letter to the right person.
phase5.game: The prototype's loop sends WM_KEYDOWN to WndProc, which moves the player rectangle.

phase5.what: Like GetMessage but never waits — lets a game loop keep running.
phase5.def: PeekMessage checks the message queue and returns immediately whether or not a message is available, optionally removing it.
phase5.model: _kbhit for windows: anything for me? No? Fine — run a frame.
phase5.game: The prototype switches to PeekMessage so the game updates every frame even when you're not touching the keys.
phase5.gameCode:
while (PeekMessage(&msg, NULL, 0, 0, PM_REMOVE)) DispatchMessage(&msg);
update(dt); render();

phase5.what: Your function Windows calls with each message: WM_KEYDOWN, WM_PAINT, WM_DESTROY…
phase5.def: A window procedure is a callback the system calls to process messages for a window, returning a result for each.
phase5.model: Your window's receptionist: every event knocks on its door.
phase5.game: WM_KEYDOWN sets which keys are held; WM_DESTROY ends the program when you click X.

phase5.what: Tells Windows part of the window needs repainting (sends WM_PAINT).
phase5.def: InvalidateRect marks all or part of a window's client area as needing repainting, causing a WM_PAINT message.
phase5.model: Putting up a "wet paint, redo me" sign.
phase5.game: After moving the player, invalidate so WM_PAINT draws the rectangle in its new place.

phase5.what: Windows libraries that hold the window and drawing functions. Link them.
phase5.def: user32.lib and gdi32.lib are import libraries that let the linker resolve calls into the Windows user-interface and graphics DLLs.
phase5.model: Library cards for the Windows kitchens that actually make windows and draw shapes.
phase5.game: Without them the prototype compiles but can't link CreateWindowEx or FillRect.

phase5.what: Measure how long each frame really took, instead of trusting Sleep.
phase5.def: Frame time is the measured duration of one loop iteration, typically from a high-resolution counter such as QueryPerformanceCounter.
phase5.model: A stopwatch on every lap instead of guessing how long a lap takes.
phase5.game: Measure dt each frame and the player moves the same speed on every PC.

phase5.what: Draw to an off-screen bitmap, then copy it to the window in one go.
phase5.def: Double buffering draws a frame to an off-screen surface, then copies it to the screen in one operation to avoid flicker.
phase5.model: The runner's char frame buffer, made of pixels.
phase5.game: The prototype draws player and obstacles into a back bitmap, then BitBlts it to the window.

phase6.what: Seconds since last frame. Multiply speeds by it so movement is the same at any fps.
phase6.example: x += speed * dt;   // speed in pixels/second
phase6.def: Delta time is the elapsed time since the previous frame, used to scale per-frame changes into per-second rates.
phase6.model: Paying by the hour, not by the visit. A fast PC visits more often but earns the same per hour.
phase6.game: x += speed * dt moves the player 300 pixels a second at 60 fps or 144 fps.

phase6.what: Two axis-aligned boxes overlap if they overlap on x and on y.
phase6.example:
a.x < b.x + b.w && a.x + a.w > b.x &&
a.y < b.y + b.h && a.y + a.h > b.y
phase6.def: An axis-aligned bounding box test detects overlap between two rectangles by comparing their extents on each axis.
phase6.model: Two boxes touch only if their shadows overlap on the floor and on the wall.
phase6.game: Player box versus obstacle box — overlap ends the run.
phase6.gameCode:
bool hit = a.x < b.x + b.w && a.x + a.w > b.x &&
           a.y < b.y + b.h && a.y + a.h > b.y;

phase6.what: Change state once, at the end of the frame, so no code runs twice.
phase6.def: Deferring a state change to the end of the frame ensures all of this frame's logic runs under one consistent state.
phase6.model: Finish the current turn before switching to the next player.
phase6.game: A hit sets next_state = GAME_OVER; the switch finishes the frame, then the change applies.

phase6.what: Update changes the game; render only draws it. Pause = skip update, keep render.
phase6.def: Separating update (changing game state) from render (drawing it) lets each run at its own rate and keeps drawing free of side effects.
phase6.model: The referee decides what happened; the camera only films it.
phase6.game: Pause skips update but keeps render, so the paused screen still draws.

phase6.what: GDI functions that draw text in the window — for the score.
phase6.def: TextOut and DrawText are GDI functions that draw a string into a device context at a position or within a rectangle.
phase6.model: A label printer for your window.
phase6.game: Drawing "Score: 12" in the corner of the prototype's window instead of the console.
